title: iDb-RRT: Sampling-based Kinodynamic Motion Planning with Motion Primitives and Trajectory Optimization

elements.name: Kinodynamic Motion Planning Problem
elements.description: The problem of finding collision-free trajectories in high-dimensional continuous spaces while respecting dynamic constraints and actuation limits, framed as finding sequences of states and controls that satisfy discretized dynamics, bounds, and boundary conditions.
elements.source_text: Kinodynamic motion planning is a fundamental problem in robotics where the goal is to find collision-free trajectories in high-dimensional, continuous, and non-convex spaces, while also considering actuation limits and dynamics of the robot.

elements.name: Discontinuity Bounded Solution
elements.description: A trajectory that approximately satisfies the dynamics constraints with a bounded violation delta. The next state need not exactly equal step(x_k, u_k), but must be within delta distance. Similarly start and goal states need only be within delta of x_s and x_g. This concept enables planning with motion primitives that do not connect exactly.
elements.source_text: Definition 1 (Discontinuity Bounded Solution): A trajectory X = (x_0, ..., x_K), U = (u_0, ..., u_{K-1}) is a delta-discontinuity bounded solution of the kinodynamic motion planning problem Eq. (3) if: d(x_{k+1}, step(x_k, u_k)) <= delta, d(x_0, x_s) <= delta, d(x_K, x_g) <= delta, x_k in X_free and u_k in U, where d(., .) is a distance function, e.g., a weighted Euclidean norm, and delta >= 0.

elements.name: Motion Primitive
elements.description: A precomputed short, dynamically feasible trajectory segment connecting a start state to a final state with associated cost. Primitives are generated offline by sampling random start/goal pairs and solving via nonlinear trajectory optimization. They can be adapted on-the-fly using system properties like translation invariance.
elements.source_text: Definition 2 (Motion Primitive): A motion primitive m = (X, U, x_s, x_f, c) is a sequence of states X = (x_0, ..., x_N), x_k in X, and controls U = (u_0, ..., u_{N-1}), u_k in U that fulfill the dynamics x_{k+1} = step(x_k, u_k). It connects the start state x_s = x_0 and the final state x_f = x_N, with a corresponding cost c in R+. The length of the motion primitive (i.e., the number of states and controls) is randomized.
elements.pseudocode: Primitive structure: (states=[x_0..x_N], controls=[u_0..u_{N-1}], start_state=x_s, final_state=x_f, cost=c)

elements.name: Feasibility-driven DDP
elements.description: A variant of Differential Dynamic Programming (DDP) that can be warm-started with an infeasible sequence of states and controls. Provides a good balance between local convergence and globalization, making it suitable for optimizing discontinuous trajectories from Db-RRT.
elements.source_text: In particular, we use the optimization algorithm Feasibility-driven DDP [39], which can be warm-started with an infeasible sequence of states and controls, providing a good balance between local convergence and globalization.

elements.name: Bidirectional Db-RRT (Db-RRT-Connect)
elements.description: A bidirectional search variant that grows two trees in parallel: one from the start state using forward motion primitives and one from the goal state using reversed motion primitives. The trees are connected when two of their states are within the discontinuity bound delta.
elements.source_text: Inspired by RRT-Connect [3], we present a bidirectional variant of Db-RRT, where we grow two trees, one from the start (using standard motion primitives) and one from the goal (using reversed motion primitives), and attempt to connect them. The expansion step in a backward search mirrors that of a forward search but requires reversing the order of states and controls in the motion primitives beforehand. The two trees are connected if two of their states are within the discontinuity bound.
elements.pseudocode:
Grow tree_from_start using standard primitives
Grow tree_from_goal using reversed primitives
Connect when nearest states are within delta

elements.name: Voronoi Bias in RRT Expansion
elements.description: The property that nodes at the frontier of the RRT search tree are more likely to be selected for expansion, causing rapid exploration of the feasible state space. Db-RRT inherits this property from the standard RRT nearest-neighbor nearest expansion mechanism.
elements.source_text: This approach provides a Voronoi bias (i.e., nodes at the frontier of the search tree are more likely to get expanded), thus rapidly exploring the feasible state space.

elements.name: Continuous Dynamics
elements.description: The continuous-time dynamics of the robot modeled as a differential equation x_dot = f(x, u), where x is the state and u is the control input.
elements.source_text: $$\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}). \tag{1}$$

elements.name: Discretized Dynamics (Euler Integration)
elements.description: Zero-order hold discretization of the continuous dynamics using Euler approximation: x_{k+1} = x_k + f(x_k, u_k) * dt. This defines the step function used throughout the algorithm.
elements.source_text: $$\mathbf{x}_{k+1} \approx \text{step}(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) \equiv \mathbf{x}_k + \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) \Delta t$$

elements.name: Kinodynamic Motion Planning Problem
elements.description: The formal optimization/search problem: find a sequence of controls U, states X, and horizon K that satisfies dynamics constraints, control bounds, collision-free state constraints, and boundary conditions (start and goal states).
elements.source_text:
find $$\mathbf{U}, \mathbf{X}, K$$
 (3a)

s.t. 
$$\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = \text{step}(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) \quad \forall k \in \{0, \dots, K-1\},$$
 (3b)

$$\mathbf{u}_k \in \mathcal{U} \qquad \forall k \in \{0, \dots, K-1\}, \quad (3c)$$

$$\mathbf{x}_k \in \mathcal{X}_{\text{free}} \subseteq \mathcal{X} \qquad \forall k \in \{0, \dots, K\}, \quad (3d)$$

$$\mathbf{x}_0 = \mathbf{x}_s; \ \mathbf{x}_K = \mathbf{x}_q. \tag{3e}$$
elements.pseudocode:
Find U, X, K such that:
  x_{k+1} = step(x_k, u_k) for all k
  u_k in U_bounds for all k
  x_k in X_free for all k
  x_0 = x_s, x_K = x_q

elements.name: Trajectory Cost Function
elements.description: The cost function used to evaluate trajectories a posteriori. For minimal time: j(u_k, x_k) = 1. For minimal control effort: j(u_k, x_k) = ||u_k||^2. Total cost J = sum of j(u_k, x_k) * dt.
elements.source_text: We use the cost term $J(\mathbf{U}, \mathbf{X}) = \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} j(\mathbf{u}_k, \mathbf{x}_k) \, \Delta t$ , with $j(\mathbf{u}_k, \mathbf{x}_k) = 1$  for minimal time (span) (alternatively, one might use $j(\mathbf{u}_k, \mathbf{x}_k) = \|\mathbf{u}_k\|^2$  for minimal control effort).
elements.pseudocode:
J = sum_{k=0}^{K-1} j(u_k, x_k) * dt
  where j(u_k, x_k) = 1 (time) or ||u_k||^2 (control effort)

elements.name: Discontinuity Bound Decrease Schedule
elements.description: The discontinuity bound decreases geometrically: d_i = d_{i-1} * d_r, where d_r < 1 is a fixed rate. Used when trajectory optimization fails to repair discontinuities.
elements.source_text: We decrease the allowed discontinuity following a geometric sequence, $d_i = d_{i-1} \cdot d_r$  with a fixed rate $d_r < 1$

elements.name: Primitive Count Increase Schedule
elements.description: The number of motion primitives increases geometrically: m_i = m_{i-1} * m_r, where m_r > 1 is a fixed rate. Used when the search fails to find a solution within the timeout.
elements.source_text: and increase the number of primitives also following a geometric sequence $m_i = m_{i-1} \cdot m_r$  with a fixed rate $m_r > 1$ .

elements.name: Trajectory Optimization Problem
elements.description: The nonlinear trajectory optimization problem that repairs discontinuities from Db-RRT. Minimizes cost including collision/goal penalties via squared penalty method and max activation for inequalities, subject to dynamics constraints and fixed start state. Solved with Feasibility-driven DDP.
elements.source_text:
$$\min_{\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{U}} \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} c(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) + c_K(\mathbf{x}_K),$$
 (4a)

s.t. 
$$\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = \text{step}(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) \quad \forall k \in \{0, \dots, K-1\},$$
 (4b)

$$\mathbf{x}_0 = \mathbf{x}_s \,. \tag{4c}$$
elements.pseudocode:
min_{X, U} sum_{k=0}^{K-1} c(x_k, u_k) + c_K(x_K)
  s.t. x_{k+1} = step(x_k, u_k) for all k
  x_0 = x_s
  c includes: collision penalty, goal penalty, control regularization, acceleration regularization

elements.name: iDb-RRT: Iterative Discontinuity Bounded RRT
elements.description: The main outer-loop algorithm that iteratively runs Db-RRT search and trajectory optimization. If search fails (timeout), increases the number of motion primitives. If optimization fails, decreases the discontinuity bound delta. Terminates when a feasible trajectory is found.
elements.source_text:
Algorithm 1: iDb-RRT Iterative Discontinuity Bounded RRT
Input: x_s, x_g, step, X_free, U, M_L
Result: X, U
1 delta <- delta_0
2 M <- ChoosePrimitives(M_L)
while not found do
3   X_d, U_d <- db-RRT(x_s, x_g, X_free, M, delta)
4   if X_d, U_d successfully computed then
5     X, U <- Optimization(X_d, U_d, x_s, x_q, step, X_free, U)
6     if X, U successfully computed then Return (X, U)
7     delta <- DecreaseDelta(delta)
8   delta <- DecreaseDelta(delta)
9   M <- IncreasePrimitives(M, M_L)
elements.pseudocode:
delta = delta_0        # initial discontinuity bound
M = ChoosePrimitives(M_L)  # initial subset of primitives
while not found:
    (X_d, U_d) = db_RRT(x_s, x_g, X_free, M, delta)
    if (X_d, U_d) successfully computed:
        (X, U) = Optimization(X_d, U_d, x_s, x_g, step, X_free, U)
        if (X, U) successfully computed:
            return (X, U)  # feasible solution found
        delta = DecreaseDelta(delta)  # optimization failed, reduce delta
    delta = DecreaseDelta(delta)  # search failed or timeout
    M = IncreasePrimitives(M, M_L)  # add more primitives

elements.name: Db-RRT: Discontinuity Bounded RRT
elements.description: The core RRT search algorithm adapted to use motion primitives with bounded discontinuity. Uses goal bias to occasionally sample toward the goal. On each step: find nearest tree node, expand using motion primitives, add new node if close enough to goal or sufficiently separated from existing nodes.
elements.source_text:
Algorithm 2: Db-RRT - Rapidly-Exploring Random Trees with Motion Primitives
Input: x_s, x_g, X_free, M, delta
Result: X_d, U_d
1 T <- AddNode(x_s)
while not TerminateCondition() do
2   if rand() < goalBias then
3     x_rand <- x_g
4   else
5     x_rand <- Sample(X_free)
6     x_nearest <- Nearest(T, x_rand)
7     x_new, m <- ExpandDb(x_nearest, x_rand, X_free, M, delta)
8     if x_new != NULL then
9       if d(x_new, x_g) < delta then
10        T <- AddNode(T, x_new)
11        X_d, U_d <- TracebackTrajectory(T, x_new)
12        Return(X_d, U_d)
13       else if NearestDistance(T, x_new) > delta then
14        T <- AddNode(T, x_new)

elements.name: Expand-Db Focused
elements.description: Focused expansion strategy that selects the motion primitive bringing the state closest to the target from a finite set of nearby candidates. Uses NearestR to find primitives close to the origin state, evaluates each for collision-freeness, and picks the one whose final state is closest to the target.
elements.source_text:
Algorithm 3: Expand-Db: Focused
Input: x_o, x_t, X_free, M, delta
Result: x, m
1 M_c <- NearestR(x_o, M, delta)
2 m_b = NULL, d_b = infinity
3 for m in M_c do
4   if m in X_free and d(m.x_f, x_t) < d_b then
5     m_b <- m,    d_b <- d(m.x_f, x_t)
6 if m_b != NULL then
7   Return m_b.x_f, m_b
8 Return NULL, NULL

elements.name: Expand-Db Randomized
elements.description: Uninformed expansion strategy that returns the first collision-free primitive found from a random permutation of candidates. Less computationally expensive than focused expansion since it stops at the first valid primitive rather than evaluating all candidates.
elements.source_text:
Algorithm 4: Expand-Db: Randomized
Input: x_o, x_t, X_free, M, delta
Result: x, m
1 M_c <- NearestR(x_o, M, delta)
2 for m in RandomPermutation(M_c) do
3   if m in X_free then
4     Return m.x_f, m
5 Return NULL, NULL

elements.name: Probabilistic Completeness of iDb-RRT
elements.description: Proof that iDb-RRT is probabilistically complete: the probability of finding a solution, if one exists, converges to 1. The proof relies on Db-RRT inheriting RRT's probabilistic completeness via its Voronoi-biased expansion, and the iterative increase of primitives and decrease of discontinuity bound ensuring the preconditions are eventually met.
elements.source_text: The RRT algorithm is probabilistically complete [22], [40], that is, the probability of eventually finding a solution, if one exists, converges to one. ... Next, we consider iDb-RRT (Algorithm 1). If Db-RRT fails to find a solution because at least one precondition is violated (a large M^L and delta < delta_1), we adjust both parameters and repeat (Lines 12 to 13), yielding a non-zero probability of executing Db-RRT with parameters that fulfill our assumptions. Finally, we assume that there exists a delta such that if Db-RRT generates a delta-discontinuity bounded solution, the trajectory optimization algorithm will converge with a non-zero probability, which makes our algorithm, iDb-RRT, probabilistically complete.

elements.name: Dynobench 30-Problem Benchmark
elements.description: Evaluation of iDb-RRT on 30 problems spanning 8 different dynamical systems (Unicycle 1, Unicycle 2, Car with trailer, Acrobot, Quadrotor v0, Quadrotor v1, Planar rotor, Rotor pole) in various environments including 14 additional complex scenarios with more obstacles requiring longer trajectories. Algorithms tested 20 times with different random seeds, reporting median compute time and cost.
elements.source_text: We evaluate iDb-RRT on 30 problems that include 8 different dynamical systems in various environments. The first 16 problems are inspired by previous work on kinodynamic motion planning [26], [23], [41], [42] (selected problems in [20], first 16 rows in Table I). Furthermore, we include 14 additional problems with the same dynamical systems but in larger, more complex environments with more obstacles, which require longer trajectories (last 14 rows in Table I).

elements.name: Comparison Against Baselines (Kino-RRT, Geo-RRT-TO, iDb-A*)
elements.description: Comparison of iDb-RRT-F (forward) and iDb-RRT-C (bidirectional) against Kino-RRT (OMPL kinodynamic RRT), Geo-RRT-TO (geometric RRT + trajectory optimization), and iDb-A* (iterative search with motion primitives). Results show iDb-RRT-F achieves 100% success rate on 28/30 problems and iDb-RRT-C on 28/30. iDb-RRT-C is fastest in 19 problems, iDb-RRT-F in 6.
elements.source_text: iDb-RRT-F and iDb-RRT-C solve all problems with a success rate of 100% (except two problems each, where they achieve 80-90% success rate), outperforming all baseline algorithms in terms of compute time to generate a solution (e.g., iDb-RRT-C is the fastest in 19 problems, and iDb-RRT-F is the fastest in 6 problems).

elements.name: Forward vs Bidirectional Search Analysis
elements.description: Comparison between the two iDb-RRT variants showing iDb-RRT-C (bidirectional) outperforms iDb-RRT-F (forward) in 21 out of 30 problems in terms of compute time, consistent with RRT-Connect results in robotics literature.
elements.source_text: Comparing our two variants, we observe that iDb-RRT-C is better in 21 out of 30 problems in terms of compute time. These results agree with previous experiments in the RRT literature, where RRT-Connect is generally faster than a forward search (in robotics problems, starting a search from the start and the goal is often beneficial because these configurations are often close to obstacles and narrow passages).

elements.name: Time Discretization dt
elements.description: The time step for Euler integration. Value depends on the system: dt = 0.1 s for car-like robots, dt = 0.01 s for flying robots and the Acrobot. Can be reduced to 0.05 s for a 5x speedup in trajectory optimization.
elements.source_text: All systems use explicit Euler integration (2), with Delta t = 0.1 s for all car-like robots and Delta t = 0.01 s for the flying robots and the Acrobot.

elements.name: Initial Discontinuity Bound delta_0
elements.description: The initial discontinuity bound delta that defines how much dynamic constraint violation is allowed during the search phase. System-dependent: Unicycle 1 v0 uses 0.3, Quadcopter v0 uses 0.35, Rotor pole uses 0.45. Computed with a weighted Euclidean norm (e.g., weight 1 for position, 0.5 for orientation).
elements.source_text: As a reference, for the system Unicycle 1 v0, we use an initial set of 200 primitives and an initial discontinuity bound of 0.3. The discontinuity is computed with a weighted Euclidean norm (e.g., weight 1 for position and 0.5 for orientation); thus a delta of 0.3 could represent up to 30 cm of discontinuity in position or 0.6 rad in orientation.

elements.name: Initial Motion Primitive Count
elements.description: The number of motion primitives used initially, before geometric increase. System-dependent: 200 for Unicycle 1 v0, 5000 for Quadcopter v0, 8000 for Rotor pole. More primitives are needed for higher-dimensional state spaces.
elements.source_text: For the Quadcopter v0, we use 5000 primitives and a discontinuity bound of 0.35, and for the Rotor pole, we use 8000 motions and a discontinuity bound of 0.45.

elements.name: Goal Bias Probability
elements.description: The probability of sampling the goal state instead of a random state during RRT expansion. A small probability that biases the tree toward the goal, improving convergence speed.
elements.source_text: With a small probability (the so-called goal bias), we expand towards the goal state instead of a random state.
elements.pseudocode:
goalBias = small probability (e.g., 0.05-0.1)
if rand() < goalBias: sample goal else: sample random state

elements.name: Discontinuity Decrease Rate d_r and Primitive Increase Rate m_r
elements.description: Geometric sequences for adjusting difficulty: d_r < 1 controls how fast the discontinuity bound shrinks (e.g., multiplied by d_r each iteration), m_r > 1 controls how fast more primitives are added to the pool.
elements.source_text: We decrease the allowed discontinuity following a geometric sequence, $d_i = d_{i-1} \cdot d_r$  with a fixed rate $d_r < 1$ , and increase the number of primitives also following a geometric sequence $m_i = m_{i-1} \cdot m_r$  with a fixed rate $m_r > 1$ .
elements.pseudocode: d_r < 1, m_r > 1  (geometric rates for delta decrease and primitive increase)

elements.name: Compute Time Analysis of iDb-RRT Components
elements.description: Analysis showing trajectory optimization dominates total compute time. For flying robots: 1-3s per optimization. For car-like robots: 50-200ms per optimization. The paper also reports speedup achievable by reducing time discretization from 0.01s to 0.05s (expected 5x speedup).
elements.source_text: In iDb-RRT, the time spent in trajectory optimization dominates the total compute time. For instance, the compute time required to optimize one trajectory in the new benchmark problems with flying robots is between 1s and 3s, while in car-like robots is between 50ms and 200ms.
